title: When to use a log axis
objectives: Choose between a linear and a log price axis for a long history
Read percentage moves off a log axis and spot the values it hides

screens.title: Which fall was worst?

screens.question: Tap the trough that ended the biggest **percentage** fall.

hints.text: Turn each fall into a share of its peak.
The 2002 trough is £200.00, after a peak of £400.00.
From £400.00 to £200.00 is a 50% fall. 2008 fell from £900.00 to £585.00, which is 35%.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Divide each trough by its peak before you compare.

byKey.t08: You picked the fall that looks biggest. It lost the most pounds, £315.00, but that is 35% of £900.00. 2002 lost 50%.
byKey.t20: That drop looks tall because prices were high by 2020. £1,500.00 to £1,200.00 is a 20% fall.

explain.text: You compared shares of each peak, not heights on the chart. 2002 fell 50%, 2008 fell 35% and 2020 fell 20%. On an ordinary axis the early fall looks tiny because the prices were small.

options.text: It stays the same
It gets steeper
options.why: That is the top chart. On an ordinary axis a doubling from £150 adds £150, six times the rise from £25.

options.text: It gets flatter
options.why: Higher up the bottom axis the gridlines bunch together, but the line keeps its slope. Drag again and watch it.

feedback.correct: Every doubling has the same height on the bottom chart.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Drag the start point and watch the bottom line only.

explain.text: On the bottom axis, every doubling climbed the same height wherever you dragged the start. On the top one, the same +100% grew taller as the price grew. The bottom axis measures moves as ratios.

screens.title: Measuring on a log axis
screens.prose: An axis where equal steps multiply the price is a **log axis**: the height of a price is proportional to its logarithm. On this one, the gap from £100 to £200 is 2 cm tall on the screen.
screens.question: How tall is the gap from £200 to £800?

widget.label: Height in cm
widget.accept: 4 cm: £200 to £800 is two doublings, and each doubling is 2 cm.

hints.text: How many doublings take £200 to £800?
£200 to £400 is one doubling; £400 to £800 is another.
Two doublings at 2 cm each make 4 cm.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count doublings, not pounds.

byKey.linear: You scaled by pounds: £600 is six times £100. On a log axis only the ratio counts.
byKey.ratio: You multiplied 2 cm by the ratio 4. A ratio of 4 is two doublings, so it is 2 × 2 cm.
byKey.one: That is one doubling. £200 to £800 multiplies by 4, which is two doublings.

explain.text: You counted ratios: ×4 is two doublings, so 4 cm. On a log axis the height of a move depends only on the ratio, never on the pounds.

screens.title: One line of matplotlib
screens.prose:
Here is the fund's history on a log axis. We want matplotlib to draw it like this, with the prices still labelled in pounds.

```python
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 4.5))
ax.plot(years, closes)
```
screens.question: Which line comes next?

options.text: `ax.set_yscale("log")`
`ax.plot(years, np.log(closes))`
options.why: That plots the logs themselves. The shape is right, but the ticks read 4.6 and 7.4 instead of £100 and £1,600.

options.text: `ax.set_ylim("log")`
options.why: `set_ylim` sets the range of the axis, two numbers. The scale is a separate setting.

options.text: `ax.loglog(years, closes)`
options.why: That logs the x axis too, which squeezes the years together. Only the prices need a log scale.

hints.text: The axis changes, not the data.
The method name matches what `ax.get_yscale()` reads back.
`ax.set_yscale("log")` keeps the prices and changes how the axis spaces them.

feedback.correct: The prices stay in pounds and the axis spaces them by ratio.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Change the y axis's scale and leave the data alone.

explain.text: `set_yscale("log")` changes only the axis, so tick labels still read in pounds. Taking `np.log` of the data gives the same shape with unreadable labels. Now the three falls show their true sizes.

screens.title: A zero goes missing
screens.prose:
A strategy's cumulative P&L in £ over five days, on an ordinary axis. A colleague switches it to a log axis.

```python
ax.plot([0.00, 120.50, -80.25, 310.00, 450.75])
ax.set_yscale("log")
```
screens.question: How many of the five values can appear on the log axis?

hints.text: Where on a log axis would £0 sit?
Each step down halves the price, and halving never reaches zero.
The £0.00 and the −£80.25 have no place on the axis. Three values remain.

feedback.correct: Only the three positive values survive.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. A log axis has room only for numbers above zero.

byKey.all: You expected matplotlib to draw every value. It drops zero and negatives without an error.
byKey.four: The zero goes, but so does the −£80.25. A log axis has no negative numbers either.
byKey.none: matplotlib does not refuse the plot. It quietly drops the values it cannot place.

explain.text: The log axis has no zero and no negatives, so £0.00 and −£80.25 vanish. matplotlib gives no error: the line simply breaks. A chart that starts at zero or crosses it needs an ordinary axis.

screens.title: Your log chart
screens.prose: Finish `log_chart` so it draws the closes on a log axis labelled `Price (£)`. Plot the prices themselves, not their logs.
screens.question: Complete `log_chart(years, closes)`.

widget.starter:
import matplotlib
matplotlib.use("Agg")  # draw to files, not a window
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt


def log_chart(years, closes):
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 4.5))
    ax.plot(years, closes)
    # give the y axis a log scale and the label "Price (£)"

    return fig, ax
widget.solution:
import matplotlib
matplotlib.use("Agg")  # draw to files, not a window
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt


def log_chart(years, closes):
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 4.5))
    ax.plot(years, closes)
    ax.set_yscale("log")
    ax.set_ylabel("Price (£)")
    return fig, ax
widget.how: Check runs 3 hidden tests on the figure your function returns. The first run loads matplotlib, a large package, so it can take up to 20 seconds; later runs are quick.

hints.text: Two lines go where the comment is.
One sets the scale; the other sets the y label.
Add `ax.set_yscale("log")` and `ax.set_ylabel("Price (£)")`.

feedback.correct: A log axis, labelled in pounds, over the raw prices.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Read the failing test: it names the property it checked.

explain.text: Your two lines change the axis and its label; the line still holds the raw prices. The third test checks exactly that, so `np.log(closes)` would fail it.

screens.title: Same height, same money?
screens.prose: On this log chart, rise A takes the price from £100 to £200 and rise B from £800 to £1,600. They look the same height. You held one unit of the fund through each rise.
screens.question: Which rise made you more money?

options.text: B
The same: the two rises are the same height
options.why: You read equal heights as equal pounds. On a log axis equal heights mean equal ratios: both doubled.

options.text: A
options.why: A doubled £100 into £200, a gain of £100. B also doubled, but from £800.

hints.text: What does equal height mean on a log axis?
Both rises are ×2.
A gains £100. B gains £800.

feedback.correct: B gained £800 and A gained £100, though both doubled.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Work out each gain in pounds.

byKey.same: You read equal heights as equal pounds. On a log axis equal heights mean equal ratios: each rise doubled the price. In pounds, B made £800 and A made £100.

explain.text: Equal heights on a log axis mean equal percentage moves: both rises are +100%. In pounds, B made eight times what A made. Read percentages off a log chart, and pounds off an ordinary one.

screens.title: Why every doubling looks the same
screens.prose: You saw that every doubling climbs the same height. A log axis places a price $p$ at a height proportional to $\ln p$. Put the lines in order to show why a move from $p$ to $kp$ has a height that ignores $p$.
screens.question: Put the lines of the derivation in order.

lines.text: Height of the move $= \ln(kp) - \ln p$, top minus bottom
$= \ln k + \ln p - \ln p$, since $\ln(ab) = \ln a + \ln b$
$= \ln k$, the two $\ln p$ terms cancel

hints.text: Start from the definition of the height.
Split the log of a product into a sum.
Top minus bottom, then $\ln(kp) = \ln k + \ln p$, then cancel.

feedback.correct: The height is $\ln k$: it depends on the ratio alone.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Begin with top minus bottom, then use the product rule for logs.

byKey.split: The product rule rewrites a height you have already written down. Start with top minus bottom.
byKey.k: The cancelling comes last, once both $\ln p$ terms are on the line.

explain.text: Every doubling has $k = 2$, so every doubling is $\ln 2$ tall, wherever it starts. A fall to half is $\ln 0.5 = -\ln 2$: the same height downwards. That is why a log axis compares percentage moves fairly.

screens.title: Choosing the axis
screens.prose: You are drawing the charts for a research note. A log axis suits a series whose moves we compare as percentages, and which stays above zero.

state.caption: 30 years of the index fund, log axis

screens.question: Select all that apply: which charts should use a log y axis?

options.text: The index fund's price from 1994 to 2024, £100.00 to £1,640.00
A stock that rose from £2.00 to £180.00 over 15 years
A strategy's cumulative P&L in £, starting at £0.00
options.why: P&L starts at zero and can go negative. A log axis would drop those values without a word.

options.text: A drawdown series, from 0% down to −35%
options.why: Drawdowns are zero or negative, so none of them fit on a log axis.

options.text: One month of a price that stayed between £98.00 and £104.00
options.why: Over a 6% range a log axis looks almost identical to an ordinary one. It adds an unfamiliar axis and shows nothing new.

hints.text: Two questions per chart: does it stay above zero, and does it span a big ratio?
P&L and drawdown touch or cross zero.
Only the two long price histories span big ratios and stay positive.

feedback.correct: Long, positive price histories get a log axis.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Rule out anything at or below zero, then anything over a narrow range.

byKey.pnl: P&L starts at £0.00, which has no place on a log axis.
byKey.dd: A drawdown is never above zero, so a log axis can show none of it.
byKey.month: Over £98.00 to £104.00 the two axes look the same. Keep the ordinary one.

explain.text: You kept the series that span big ratios and stay positive: long price histories. P&L, returns and drawdowns sit at or below zero, so they need an ordinary axis.

ideas: On a log axis equal heights mean equal ratios, so a 50% fall looks the same size in 1990 or 2020.
`ax.set_yscale("log")` changes the axis and keeps the tick labels in pounds; plotting `np.log(prices)` does not.
A log axis has no zero and no negatives. matplotlib drops such values silently, so P&L, returns and drawdowns keep an ordinary axis.
